draft.title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes
card: Atomic number
the number of protons in an atom. It decides which element the atom is.
Mass number
the number of protons plus the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
Isotopes
atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They have different mass numbers.
To find the neutrons in an atom, subtract the atomic number from the mass number.
draft.remember: Protons name the element. Neutrons can vary, and that makes isotopes.

a.q: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. What is its mass number?
a.why: Mass number is protons plus neutrons, so 6 + 8 = 14. The number 6 is the atomic number, and 2 comes from wrongly subtracting.
a.clue: Add the particles in the nucleus.

b.q: A lab tests two samples of neon. Atoms in sample P have 10 protons and 10 neutrons. Atoms in sample Q have 10 protons and 12 neutrons. What is true of P and Q?
opts: They are isotopes of the same element
They have the same mass number
b.why: Both have 10 protons, so they are the same element. Their neutrons differ, so they are isotopes with mass numbers 20 and 22. A different number of neutrons does not make a different element.
b.clue: Compare the protons first, then the neutrons.

b.best: They are isotopes of the same element

problems.detail: The stem calls both samples 'neon', which tells students they are the same element. That rules out 'different atomic numbers' and 'two different elements' without any need to compare protons. Describe them as 'two samples of a gas' or 'two atoms' instead.

check.summary: The card and both answers are correct. In question b, calling both samples 'neon' reveals that they are the same element and makes two distractors too easy to rule out.
